title: The Field of Unconsidered Divisions

features.name: the fractured boundary
features.desc-on-touch: Where one field becomes two becomes many. The boundary line keeps multiplying as you look at it—no single border, but a plurality of thresholds, each one claiming to be the real division.

features.name: forgotten plural counting
features.desc-on-touch: Furrows multiply under your gaze. Where there was one row of crops, you now see three. Where there were three, nine. The field was always this plural—it just waited for no one to be looking.

features.name: the silenced plural
features.desc-on-touch: Here the field whispers in voices it was never supposed to have. Singular field-names split into multiples of themselves—Place becomes Places, Memory becomes Memories, all the words the farmer's records forgot to count.

features.name: the corner no one claimed
features.desc-on-touch: A corner of the field that belonged to neither property, neither owner, neither use. It grew whatever it wanted because it was never counted. Now the archive counts it five different ways.

features.name: divided light at dusk
features.desc-on-touch: The dusk light catches the field at angles that cannot be reconciled. Each section glows in a different frequency, as if they are not one field at all but a plurality of evenings stacked.

inscription: here the field learned it had been plural all along and nobody counted it

file.name: Field_Divisions_Unrecorded_Survey.txt
file.note: A land survey from 1947 that lists field boundaries that contradict each other. Each surveyor saw the same land differently. The archive has stored all versions as equally true.

reverie.title: REVERIE — the evening the field became plural
narr: You stand in the paddock at dusk, and she points: look, this field
is not one. It never was one. The fences are lies. She shows you
how the light cuts across it in three contradictory ways, how the
soil changes where the surveyor's line said it shouldn't, how the
crops grow in secret patterns that no single farmer ever planned.
The field, she says, already knows it is many.
